run.userPrompt:
A consumer goods company sells almost entirely through third-party retailers, who control shelf placement and customer data. Management wants a direct-to-consumer channel to capture first-party data and higher margins, but its two largest retail partners together account for 55% of revenue and have punished suppliers who competed with them directly. An earlier quiet pilot of a web store triggered an angry call from one partner's buying team.

Design a go-to-market plan for building a meaningful direct-to-consumer business while keeping the retail relationships that fund the company today. Specify the channel architecture, product and pricing differentiation between channels, the data strategy, and the partner-communication plan that prevents open channel conflict.

agentResponses.content:
That angry phone call from the retail buyer… it’s a very loud, very blunt instrument, isn’t it? It tells us exactly what they fear: a zero-sum game for the same margin. Our earlier pilot failed because, even in its quietness, it was still fundamentally just a store. It was a digital mirror of the retail shelf. When we try to play the same game on a different board, the incumbents will always use their weight to flip the table. But what if we stop trying to build a better shelf, and instead build a completely different kind of room? 

If we look at the architecture of this new channel, perhaps we shouldn't build a traditional e-commerce funnel at all. What if we construct an "insight collective" or a "brand atelier"? A space that doesn't feel like a point of purchase, but rather a membership for our most devoted users to interact with the edges of our brand. We strip away the aggressive "add to cart" urgency and replace it with a fluid, exploratory interface. It shouldn't compete for the impulse buy; it should cater to the deep dive. By making the architecture feel more like a community hub or an innovation sandbox, we subtly signal to our retail partners—and to the consumers—that this isn't a replacement for the convenience of the aisle, but a complement to it.

Naturally, this shifts how we think about the products and the pricing within that space. If we put the exact same flagship SKUs on this digital platform, we are inviting a turf war. Instead, what if we only offer the "un-shelfable"? We could explore the negative space of our catalog: highly personalized bundles, limited-run collaborations, bespoke formulations, or a closed-loop refill ecosystem that requires direct logistics. We price these offerings at a distinct premium. Not to artificially inflate costs, but to signal that this is a tailored, high-touch experience. The retail shelf remains the accessible, immediate-gratification point for our core products, while our direct channel becomes the home for exploration and customization. We aren't undercutting our partners; we are operating in an adjacent stratosphere they simply don't have the infrastructure to support.

And then there is the data. The traditional reflex is to trade a 10% discount for an email address, but our retail partners already hoard the transactional data. Why compete on their terms? What if we seek *contextual* data instead? We don't just want to know what they bought; we want to understand the ritual of how they use it. Through subtle, interactive digital companions, quiet community forums, or beautifully designed diagnostic quizzes, we can map the daily rhythms of our users. We trade genuine value—personalized routines, early access to experiments, a sense of belonging—for their stories. This first-party data won't just tell us how to sell more; it will tell us what to invent next. It’s a much richer, more nuanced vein of gold.

But how do we manage the delicate dance with the giants who hold 55% of our revenue? We certainly don’t ask for their permission, nor do we try to hide in the shadows. Hiding just breeds suspicion. Instead, what if we reframe the entire narrative? We don't announce a "D2C pivot." We position this direct channel internally and externally as a "customer intimacy lab." When we sit down with our retail partners, we don't talk about our direct sales volume—which will be purposefully kept small and ambiguous in the early days anyway. Instead, we share the macro-trends and behavioral shifts we’re observing in our lab. We say, "Look at this fascinating new usage pattern our most engaged users are developing; you might want to adjust your end-cap displays to highlight this." We make them feel like the beneficiaries of our R&D. By feeding them synthesized insights, we turn a perceived threat into an exclusive advisory relationship. 

It requires a certain comfort with delayed gratification to let a direct channel evolve this way. The board might initially be confused by the lack of aggressive, hockey-stick D2C revenue projections, but isn't that exactly how we protect the core while quietly planting the seeds of the future? We absorb the ambiguity, let the offering organically find its resonance, and read the subtle cues of our most engaged users. 

Shall we pull together a few of our most empathetic product designers and behavioral observers for a quiet brainstorm next Tuesday? We could start by sketching out what the "un-shelfable" actually looks like for our brand, and perhaps draft the first few subtle prompts we might use to uncover the rituals of our most devoted users. We can let the shape of this new channel reveal itself, long before the retail buyers even realize the gravity of our business has gently shifted.
